title: The Crumb Inside the Atom
set_language: ONE persistent Cambridge 1897 cathode-ray lab set: long glass tube, glowing beam, magnet, charged plates, swap-in electrodes. Later beat: 1904 plum-pudding model as a clear cartoon. Say 'same 1897 Cambridge tube set'. Never 'same DNA'.
continuity_lock: No Explorer this part. Readable J.J. Thomson face (moustache, round glasses).
forbidden: HARD REJECT: Orbit robot; photoreal; Ken Burns or still push; gore; lava drip / molten bead; underside lamp bulb or shade cup; unfinished flat cards; unfinished Explorer hair; DNA helix; readable text or logos baked into the plate (labels added in edit); twin Explorer; never say 'same DNA' or 'lab DNA' in a Veo prompt. No Explorer. No Orbit.
motion_lock: Real Veo motion; Quality for tube beam glow.
quality_note: Veo 3.1 Quality for beam / glow. No lava.

plates.vo_land: Cambridge, eighteen ninety-seven. J.J. Thomson is studying a strange glow.
plates.prompt: Animistry premium 3D cartoon. Cambridge 1897 lab. J.J. Thomson (readable face, moustache, round glasses) at a long glass tube with a glowing beam. Continuous. Silent. No Explorer. HARD REJECT: Orbit, unfinished face, lava.

plates.vo_land: Pump the air out of a glass tube, run electricity through it, and a beam shoots from one end to the other. Scientists called them cathode rays. But what were they made of? Light, or stuff?
plates.prompt: Same 1897 Cambridge tube set. Beam shoots end to end; question mood. Continuous beam. Quality clean glow. Silent. HARD REJECT: Orbit, Explorer, underside bulb.

plates.vo_land: Thomson brings a magnet close. The beam bends. He tries two charged metal plates. It bends again. Light doesn't do that. Tiny charged particles do.
plates.prompt: Same tube set. Magnet approaches — beam bends; then two metal plates — bends again. Continuous bend. Silent. HARD REJECT: Orbit, Explorer, lava.

plates.vo_land: Then he measures how far they bend, and works out how heavy they must be. The answer is astonishing: far lighter than a hydrogen atom, the lightest thing anyone knew. We now know each one is about two thousand times lighter.
plates.prompt: Same tube set. Measurement of bend; crumb visual far lighter than a hydrogen ball. Continuous. Silent. HARD REJECT: Orbit, garbled dials.

plates.vo_land: But here is the strange part. It doesn't matter which metal he uses. The same particles come out every time.
plates.prompt: Same tube set. Different metal electrodes swap in; same tiny particles stream out each time. Continuous swap. Silent. HARD REJECT: Orbit, Explorer.

plates.vo_land: So the uncuttable thing can be cut. Every atom carries these tiny negative particles. Thomson called them corpuscles. Today we call them electrons.
plates.prompt: Cartoon atom cracks open; tiny negative crumbs inside. Continuous crack. Silent. HARD REJECT: Orbit, gore, DNA helix.

plates.vo_land: But atoms have no overall charge, so something positive must balance them out. A few years later, in nineteen-oh-four, Thomson made his guess: a soft ball of positive stuff with electrons dotted through it, like raisins in a pudding.
plates.prompt: Animistry premium 3D cartoon. 1904 plum pudding model: soft positive sphere with electron raisins. Continuous gentle rotate. Silent. HARD REJECT: photoreal food only, Orbit, Explorer.

plates.vo_land: It was a lovely idea. It was also wrong.
plates.prompt: Same pudding model cracks / dissolves — lovely, and wrong. Continuous fail. Silent. HARD REJECT: Orbit, Explorer, Ken Burns only.
